title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
description: Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.The government had hope
body: Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost £33bn, would open by 2035.But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025 as a means to grow the economy, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy as part of a wider £49bn modernisation of the airport.The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.A DfT spokesperson said: "There is currently no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress."The timeline has always been ambitious. We'll continue to work with promoters, including Heathrow, and all other stakeholders at pace to ensure the right framework is in place for which a planning application for a third runway could be considered."A spokesperson for Heathrow said: "It's right that ambitious targets were set; the sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit."They said the benefits would involve "at least 108,000 new jobs and billions of pounds invested in supply chains in every part of the country"."This is a national project, 100% privately financed which will support growth today and secure the UK's position in the global economy once the runway opens."Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.Correction 26 September: An earlier version of this story said the runway was estimated to cost £49bn. It has been updated to reflect that this figure is the total amount of investment planned for the airport, including £33bn for the runway.

schema.headline: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years

title: Andy Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help young people get on the property ladder.The "Your First Home" scheme would be
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help young people get on the property ladder.The "Your First Home" scheme would be open to first-time buyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their new build property's value to help pay for the purchase.Burnham said people who do not have support from the "bank of mum and dad" are among those the scheme would aim to help.There would be an initial interest-free period for the equity loan, with more details expected in next month's Budget.The Conservatives warned the policy would leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risks "pushing up the price of new homes".Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own."So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder."The PM added he believes the scheme will give builders the "confidence to deliver the high-quality new homes the country needs".Funding for the scheme is expected to come from reprioritising existing budgets, but housing developers will pay towards the running costs.Ministers have not yet confirmed whether there is an age restriction on the scheme, or a cap on the price on the value of the property.The policy is similar to initiatives from previous governments, including the coalition's Help To Buy scheme, introduced in 2013 by then-Chancellor George Osborne.It expanded a previous scheme, known as FirstBuy, which was aimed solely at first-time buyers.Help to Buy initially enabled all purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home, with a value of up to a £600,000.Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.The first version of the programme was active until 2021. A second iteration of the scheme, which ran until 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties that could be bought.An evaluation of the scheme, external found more than 387,000 properties were purchased through it, of which 328,000 were by first-time buyers.In its conclusion, the report noted Help to Buy was "effective in supporting people into home ownership in some areas, but did not remove affordability barriers for first-time buyers in areas that were already relatively expensive".Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said "Your First Home" would "build on the lessons learned from previous schemes, while retaining the benefits".The Home Builders Federation welcomed the proposals, saying it had "long called for action to improve access to home ownership"."Our analysis shows a well-designed scheme can make a meaningful difference for households struggling to get on to the property ladder," it added.Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam accused Labour of wanting first-time buyers to "take on even more debt to afford the few homes that have been built".She added taxpayers would take a "stake in their homes" and be "picking up the bill for months".Lam said: "Slapping another levy on developers risks pushing up the price of new homes too. "This is a colossal admission of failure. This Labour government is making homes harder to build, then asking buyers to borrow more to pay for them."Lam said the Conservatives want to scrap stamp duty, "back British house builders" and ensure that houses are "built in the places that people actually want to live".Rayner told the BBC earlier this month that there was only a "slim chance" the government would meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election, but said she was "not giving it up".Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.The housing policy announcement came as Burnham arrived in Liverpool ahead of his first Labour Party conference since becoming prime minister.The PM said he wanted to make it a "really important week where we set out a new direction for the country".He added: "We've had a decade since Brexit and it's been a decade of too much drift, too much division, and we need to draw a line on that."Another pre-conference announcement included a pledge to offer quicker access of a guaranteed job to young people receiving health or disability support.The offer would be made three months after they start claiming benefits. This approach would be introduced from next April.Labour said the government would cover 100% of wage costs for up to 25 hours a week for six months.Currently, jobless young people aged 18 to 24 must have been on universal credit for 18 months before receiving an offer under the government's job guarantee scheme.Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said Labour should have cut "burdens" on businesses to help ensure disabled people are employed.She said: "Instead, they are bringing back a Conservative post-pandemic scheme. Andy Burnham clearly has no new ideas."Whately also questioned how the change would be funded.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers

title: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder
description: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep
body: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep of her home on Gowan Avenue.Soon after her death, a man of Serbian descent called the BBC claiming she had been executed in a revenge hit for the UK-backed Nato bombing of Serbia's state broadcaster in Belgrade.However, Barry George, a local man, was convicted of her murder and spent eight years in jail before being acquitted at a retrial in 2008. Dando's partner, Alan Farthing, was interviewed by the police, along with her ex-partner and BBC Breakfast news editor Bob Wheaton. Also interviewed was her agent Jon Roseman, who had written a crime novel detailing a very similar scene.They were all ruled out as suspects. Her killing was the subject of a Netflix documentary Who Killed Jill Dando? in 2023.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder

title: Trump rejects Iran deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
description: US President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within a week.He told reporters at th
body: US President Donald Trump has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within a week.He told reporters at the White House that Tehran "want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly".In a post on Telegram, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's comments, but said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.On Friday, Araghchi had told reporters at the UN in New York that an agreement could be reached "if the necessary conditions are met" and that these were contained in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by the two countries in June. The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February."I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it. "They want to make a deal, and I think that's fine. I like making a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable," he added.Araghchi wrote that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently."He added that he would await the "definitive views" of mediators,  and that Tehran "will make a decision based on that."On Friday the Wall Street Journal, external cited officials as saying Trump was sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he saw a renewed bombing campaign as probable.Iran responded to US and Israeli air strikes, beginning in late February, by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz. Its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.The economic effects have also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads towards Congressional elections in November.The MOU was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including ending a US naval blockade and other sanctions. But the deal fell apart after both sides resumed strikes. Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the strait without authorisation.The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.Trump has since claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities analytics firm cited by Reuters.The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations.Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting Saudi oil exports via the Red Sea, on the other side of the Arabian peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz.The group seized strategic stretches of Yemen's Red Sea coast this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.

schema.headline: Trump rejects Iran deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days

title: Angela Rayner criticises worker visa plans on eve of Labour conference
description: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign worker
body: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.In an interview with the Times, external ahead of Labour's annual conference, Rayner questioned Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's plans, saying they are unfair because they "change the goalposts".Under the proposals, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for residency - instead of the current five - while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.Mahmood said the government would make a decision on the immigration overhaul by the end of the year.Speaking to the Times, Rayner said she was concerned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules. She described the potential rule change as "very disruptive" and added: "I do have concerns about that." During her interview with the Times, she said that the changes would impact foreign care workers who "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones". Her remarks represent direct criticism of a policy inherited by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.Rayner previously served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir, and was brought back into cabinet by Burnham in July.It is significant that a serving cabinet minister feels able to criticise an existing government proposal on the eve of Labour's conference, albeit one inherited from the Starmer era.It is part of a growing head of steam from some parts of the party to quash the retrospective elements of these plans.Rayner has previously criticised the measures. In June, she said proposals to retrospectively alter the rules for migrants already working in the UK would be "wrong". Rayner said she believed that Mahmood was aware of her position, telling the Times she has "not changed [her] view" since re-entering the cabinet.Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British". Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here. But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this month.Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

schema.headline: Angela Rayner criticises worker visa plans on eve of Labour conference

title: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue
description: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at
body: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all."It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says.These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on."Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails.In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury".But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful.Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say."That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC."They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty."For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine.Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue.For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore.Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail."It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair."Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth."I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.'"And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'."Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new.But beauty magazines have declared "All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures, external", that "Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol, external" of "Polished Women" and that "Manicures Are No Longer Classy, external".And there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it.At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya.Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year."It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home."Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says."I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money."But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister.Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro."Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC.Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour.A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman.And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement.But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say.Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Diana Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art.And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting – a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says."The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now."The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine."The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women."I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been – and continue to be - weaponised."We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"Scanlon too is a little baffled."For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't. "I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

schema.headline: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue

title: Nations League: Who made an uncharacteristic error? England player ratings v Spain
description: England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - the Three Lions' first match since this summer's Worl
body: England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - the Three Lions' first match since this summer's World Cup. Lamine Yamal gave Spain the lead before goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put England ahead. Kane then missed a penalty before Alex Baena curled in to level the score, with Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the winner. Here's how we rated England's players - and you can have your say in the comments at the bottom.James Trafford: Showed early on his ability to play with the ball at his feet but conceded after just two minutes when Guehi gifted the ball to Lamine Yamal. An important save stopped Torres making it 2-0 in the first half. 6Jarell Quansah: Continued at right-back after showing what he could do in the position at the World Cup. A physically dominant performance and had a chance to score but headed over. 6Ezri Konsa: Some shaky moments for Konsa and England's back four but the centre-back regrouped and got better as the game went on. 6 Marc Guehi: An uncharacteristic error gifted the ball - and the opening goal - to Lamine Yamal. 5Nico O'Reilly: Put in the cross for Kane's goal as England took the lead in the first half. Did a good job of trying to deal with Lamine Yamal. However he gave the ball away for Spain's second goal. 6 Elliot Anderson: Nearly punished for giving the ball away in a dangerous position in the first half but Ferran Torres rolled his shot wide. Anderson and midfield partner Lewis-Skelly took some time to settle in what was a tough night in the middle of the pitch against a Spain side who moved the ball so well. 6Myles Lewis-Skelly: A first England start in centre midfield for Lewis-Skelly after shining for Arsenal. Given the tough task of trying to shut off the supply to Spain's conductor, Rodri. A solid performance. Replaced after 70 minutes. 6Jude Bellingham: The Real Madrid midfielder produced another dominant display and was unlucky to be on the losing side. He provided an assist for England's equaliser and won a penalty which Kane hit against the bar after slipping. Stung Simon's palms with a drive in stoppage time. 8Bukayo Saka: Won a couple of free-kicks around the box and shot over from the edge of the area in the first half. Curled just wide with the score level but a quiet night for the winger. 6 Anthony Gordon: The Barcelona winger scored an excellent goal on the counter-attack. He kept calm when played through on goal by Bellingham when his pace put him clear. A dangerous cross in the first half after England went behind and a threat in behind all night. 8Harry Kane: Started dropping deep in the first half in search of the ball after England went behind. Scored the second with a deflected header to put England in the lead but missed a penalty when they had the chance to add a third in the second half. 7

schema.headline: Nations League: Who made an uncharacteristic error? England player ratings v Spain

title: Indonesia Carstensz Pyramid: Papua's 'eternal snow' on Puncak Jaya is about to disappear forever
description: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear foreverImage source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, Only smal
body: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear foreverImage source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman RangeByAbraham UtamaBBC IndonesiaThe mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.But now, nearly all the snow is gone.A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime."There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936Proof of a warming planetThe retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".Image source, Marie ŠabackáImage caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systemsA spiritual anchorAt least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow"."Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts."How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribeFor many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded. The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment."Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows ice coverage at the date of capture in 2025As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change."When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed."I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

schema.headline: Indonesia Carstensz Pyramid: Papua's 'eternal snow' on Puncak Jaya is about to disappear forever

title: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to university
description: Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on themImage source, Getty ImagesByKirstie BrewerBBC NewsLuke felt overwhelmed with
body: Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on themImage source, Getty ImagesByKirstie BrewerBBC NewsLuke felt overwhelmed with both pride and grief after dropping his son off at university for the first time."It feels like a brutal adjustment," he says."After 18 years of seeing him every day and taking care of him, I miss him so much and I don't really know what to do with myself."Like other parents we have spoken to, Luke (not his real name) and his wife have felt compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers with children living in the same halls of residence, as well as a university-wide version with more than 2,000 members.At first, being in these groups felt helpful for practical information, particularly in the weeks before his son headed to university, Luke says. But now they're feeding his anxiety."People will post things like: 'Is it normal to spend so much time in your room?'; 'I'm worried my daughter is struggling to make friends'; 'My child isn't replying to messages - how often are people hearing from theirs?'"There have also been questions about Amazon parcel logistics, requests to borrow cereal bowls and what tog duvet other people's children were given.Luke thinks these kinds of social media groups have fuelled his temptation to keep checking his son's location on a tracking app "to make sure he is going out enough and finding friends".Because his messages and calls go largely unanswered, Luke will also watch videos posted on the university's social media accounts, hoping to catch a glimpse of his son among the throngs of Freshers. Other parents have sheepishly confessed they're doing the same.Across universities, some enterprising parents have set up the sort of WhatsApp group chats you'd more typically find being used when children are at school. Only rather than asking after lost jumpers and what day PE is, these groups might be used to try to parent long-distance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some parents say they feel compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help."These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves."Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'""Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."'Students should be figuring it out for themselves'A big part of going to university is about being independent, says Manchester University student Archie Forde, 19, who has heard stories of parents "pinging phones at 3am and calling their kids 12 times a week".He thinks parents turning to social media groups have "mostly fair concerns" but are going about things in the wrong way.The groups can be "echo chambers where everyone just spins each other out about their kids", he says, and suggests having a proper conversation with your child about boundaries, before university starts.Every family will have different ideas about what is overbearing, but a student shouldn't have the worry of choosing between "cutting back parents' communication and ruining that relationship, or responding to a flurry of texts at pre-drinks and detaching yourself from the social situation".Image source, Archie FordeImage caption, Archie Forde, 19, says parents turning to social media groups are going about things in the wrong wayWriting a letter or sending a parcel - without the expectation of a getting a response - could be a good way to let your child know you're thinking of them, "without it feeling like a demand", says child psychologist Laverne Antrobus.Perhaps negotiate a time to check in with them, "and be prepared to not always have long conversations," she says.And when you do speak to your child, "make sure your curiosity is genuine, rather than half-informed by the surveillance you've been doing"."Already knowing where they've been and what they've been up to makes for an unrewarding conversation with them and children are bright - they will know."Rayyah says she looks forward to properly catching up when she goes home."If you've spent months being closely monitored it might feel as if you haven't really been away or gained any independence; it could feel frustrating."'I didn't know who I was without the kids'Having seen three children off to university, Nichola McClellan wants to reassure parents that it does get easier. Based in Cheshire, she shares her experience of being an "empty nester" on social media, external."It's a huge emotional adjustment after years of your life revolving around your children, so we need to give ourselves time and permission to miss them. "I think back to how lost I felt. I didn't know who I was without the kids. "They're learning how to leave," she says, "but we're learning how to let go."Rather than expect constant contact, Nichola sends "little no-pressure messages" on their family WhatsApp group."'Love you', 'proud of you' - things that don't require an answer."They have a proper catch-up roughly once a week, and she has learned not to take it personally if she doesn't hear from them."Sometimes that is a really good sign, it means they're getting on with this new life you've spent all those years preparing them for. "You don't stop being a parent when they leave home - but you do get the opportunity to rediscover parts of yourself that perhaps got a little lost along the way. There really is so much to look forward to."Three expert tips on letting go Psychologist Charlotte Armitage shares her advice to help parents cope with this new stage of parenthood: Think twice before you post on a parents' group Feeling anxious, bereft or excluded is normal, but those feelings don't always require action. Before posting on a group or stepping in, Armitage says ask yourself: "Is this a genuine safety issue? Have I given my young adult the chance to deal with it? Am I helping them become more capable, or managing my own anxiety?"Steer clear of constant checking and tracking or intervening These may soothe you in the short term, but can inadvertently communicate to your young adult: "I am not sure you can cope without me." Of course, parents should step in when there is a safeguarding concern or risk to their child's wellbeingThe most valuable message you can send To help your child settle into adult life, Armitage says the most valuable message you can send is: "I am here if you need me and I believe you can do this."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to university

title: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?
description: Figure caption, Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview?ByJemma Crew and Daniel ThomasBusiness reportersUpdated 11:05 BSTWould you b
body: Figure caption, Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview?ByJemma Crew and Daniel ThomasBusiness reportersUpdated 11:05 BSTWould you bring an iced coffee to a job interview?The question on the internet's lips this week started life, as many do, in a TikTok video. "Don't waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee, it just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand," said US recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen.It's what her Gen Z job candidates are doing, she said, warning it makes it look like the interview is "just a stop on your list of errands for the day".The post has started what Wehniainen calls the Great Iced Coffee Debate of 2026.Some believe turning up with an iced matcha latte in hand is a cardinal sin. They say it's unprofessional, too informal, and a distraction.Others feel this is an overreaction - distracting from how difficult it is to secure a job - or even just get an interview in the first place.In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Wehniainen says she "was never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate. "My point was simply about avoiding distractions."Can an iced latte actually hurt your chances of getting a job?What in the WorldHanad, 28, works for an energy supplier in London. He likes iced coffee but wouldn't bring one to an interview."A job interview is all about first impressions," he says. "Anything can deter the employer from employing you."Iced coffee is something a lot of teens drink… it would look immature and too informal."Image caption, Hanad says he wouldn't take an iced coffee to an interviewHe would never bring along an energy drink for the same reasons. But he says water or a hot coffee would be okay.His colleague Tsvetina, 24, thinks a potential employee shouldn't be judged by what they bring to the interview, nor their dress code."I think we should be moving away from these traditional corporate stigmas. What matters is what the person is actually communicating during the interview."Aisha, 28, says she would take along an iced coffee. "I think it shows that I have come early enough to get iced coffee."She wouldn't bring a fizzy drink, however.In general, she thinks a lot of employers like to see personality in a candidate. "It makes you stand out from other people who are coming [applying] for the job."Image caption, Katy feels there is a sexist element to the controversy around Wehniainen's postKaty, 25, a personal assistant in events, says she personally wouldn't turn up to a job interview with an iced coffee.But she sees the controversy around Wehniainen's post as "a bit sexist, because it's usually girls who drink iced coffee"."If it was a hot coffee, which is more masculine, there wouldn't be a discourse about that."Young people trying to land their first job are facing multiple challenges.The number of graduate vacancies in the UK has almost halved in the past year, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.Around one in eight people aged 16-24 are not in education, employment or training - so called Neets.Young workers in the US are also struggling with a tight jobs market, external as hiring slows.'A little bit flippant'Lucy Cooper is the founder of Spark, a design and branding recruitment company in London.She says her industry - marketing - is really tough right now, and she doesn't know of any Gen Z candidates who would risk turning up to an interview with an iced coffee.You could "seem too relaxed and a little bit flippant, like you're not taking it seriously enough, or you are interviewing the employer rather than the other way round"."I think people at junior level are very conscious about not doing anything that could jeopardise their chances," she says.She adds that it would be fine to accept a coffee offered by the employer, however, or drink one on a video interview. Dan Craddock, director at Hays, says employers shouldn't rely on "snap judgements"."It's important not to read too much into a single item a candidate brings to an interview. "Whether that's an iced coffee, a bottle of water or a notebook, employers are ultimately assessing the skills, experience and behaviours that will make someone successful in the role."Chris Mason, co-founder of Intelligent People - a specialist recruitment agency for the tech industry, says focusing on ice coffees alone "does seem to be an overreaction on the US recruiter's part".He advises candidates to "try to do everything possible to project the right image and attitude".He warns bringing snacks or specialist drinks may undermine the impression candidates will want to give - that they're "serious and focused on the interview".He says the main issue they see with some younger candidates is a lack of preparation, not being punctual, and not researching the role, organisation or interviewer.

schema.headline: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?

title: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance
description: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decen
body: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max."We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk."The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life". They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5."I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah.Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation.One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report, external by pension provider Standard Life. And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study, external by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual. Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun.She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do."Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives.Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it.He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working. "It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people."Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, , externalaccording to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity. The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows., externalBut at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, external.Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays."This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour."She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time.When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property.But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal".Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year.As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits. The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993)., external However, people can choose to take a lower payment, external from the age of 62.Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on.Back in Yorkshire, Sarah says that despite the spending, she has every intention of leaving her kids something. In the meantime she is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things."Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

schema.headline: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance

title: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob
description: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red sh
body: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red shirt, Bernard Gilbert directed a dance to song King of the Road by country singer Roger Miller in Worcester city centre, with crowds erupting in applause after he finished.The former dance teacher previously went viral on social media for his moves at Fernhill House Care Home where he lives. His videos were seen more than 1.5m times."I love the dancing, once I get on the floor I forget everything, I just concentrate on what I'm doing," he said when the BBC interviewed him in June. The flash mob in Cathedral Square featured Got2Sing choir members as well as residents as they raised money for Alzheimer's Research UK. They learnt four dances, practised hard and rehearsed at home to prepare for the event, Fernhill House Care Home said."What an inspiring day, what a community, what a fantastic memory we've created together," it added.Organisers of Got2Sing Worcester described the flash mob as a "joyful afternoon" with singers "bringing their energy and talent" to the city centre."When a 100-year-old local legend leads the line dancing, you know it's going to be a good afternoon," they said.

schema.headline: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob

title: Orange Orderparade along Garvaghy Road halted after injuction granted
description: Appeal underway after judge bans Drumcree paradeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The parade (pictured above in 2018 on a 20th anniversary prot
body: Appeal underway after judge bans Drumcree paradeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The parade (pictured above in 2018 on a 20th anniversary protest) has been halted due to a temporary injunction being granted at the High Court in Belfast.ByMichael Fitzpatrick and Catherine DoyleBBC News NIUpdated 47 minutes agoAn appeal is underway against a High Court ruling banning Portadown Orangemen from marching along the Garvaghy Road on Sunday.On Friday the Parades Commission announced that the Orange Order parade could proceed for the first time  in almost 30 years with restrictions in place.The Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition (GRRC) had mounted a legal challenge to the decision and on Saturday afternoon a High Court judge issued an injunction halting the march.The decision is being appealed, with an emergency court sitting underway. It came after Portadown District Orange Lodge declined a request from Judge Patricia Smyth to postpone the parade until all issues were properly considered.Judge Smyth, who has been hearing the legal challenge to the Parades Commission's decision, said the temporary injunction would apply until the judicial review application could be properly determined.A lawyer for the Orange Order member, who was a respondent in the case, indicated he intended to appeal the decision which is being heard at the High Court.A large crowd of residents and supporters have gathered at the Drumcree Centre off the Garvaghy Road as the Orange Orders appeal gets underway. Earlier Sínn Féin ministers Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmons were among politicians who turned up to show support.'Potential to escalate'The basis of the review was on the PSNI's risk assessment to the Parades Commission.Lawyer Denise Kiley KC for the residents told the High Court hearing that "much remains uncertain" in the wake of the ruling.She claimed that "nowhere" in the PSNI's contribution to the commission was there "any assessment of future risk" and was "entirely directed to past risk"."That all leads to a requirement for more time and for the Parades Commission to explain the discrepancy that is apparent on the face of the documents," she said.Delivering her decision to issue an injuction, Judge Smyth said "the level of mistrust" between residents and the lodge cannot be "overstated.""It is also clear to me that this particular long running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland," she added."Against that backdrop I am thoroughly of the view the issues of all three parties must be properly ventilated."Afterwards GRRC spokesperson Breandan Mac Cionnaith said that "this isn't over yet".He told supporters in a crowd of several hundred outside the High Court not to be "triumphalist".But, he added, "we're halfway there".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Breandan Mac Cionnaith outside the High Court on SaturdayReacting to developments DUP leader Gavin Robinson MP said unionists would await the court's decision and expect "all parties to respect the legal process"."The Orangemen of Portadown have conducted themselves with dignity and respect for the rule of law for 28 years. If they must wait for further deliberation, be it 28 days, they will do so with their heads held high and dignity intact."SDLP leader Claire Hanna MP said Drumcree "carries a history and a meaning that cannot be ignored". "I welcome that the heat has been taken out of this difficult episode. Lighting the tinder is easy; putting the fire out is much harder."Alliance deputy leader Eóin Tennyson MLA, said that calm heads were needed."Following the High Court's intervention, it is important that everyone now takes a step back and responds responsibly," he said.TUV leader Jim Allister said he was dismayed at the handling of the judicial review hearing."I trust the Court of Appeal will rectify the situation," he said.People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll said he would continue to offer support to Garvaghy Road residents. "We will not let them drag us back to the dark days of sectarian violence and division."'Step back from the abyss'Earlier on Saturday Judge Smyth had given the parties involved a final opportunity to "reach an agreement" and "step back from the abyss".Judge Smyth said "it is my view the issues at stake are so sensitive and so important, I would expect all of the lawyers to be creative and to use the law for the good of all the people in Northern Ireland."The judge said the issue the court is dealing with is of "fundamental importance" to the entire society in Northern Ireland.Portadown District Lodge submitted a letter in which they outlined their reasons for not agreeing to delay the parade."The suggestion there is no prejudice to us is, to be frank, absolutely contrary to all reality," the letter said."The prejudice is very clear – those opposed to us could simply ramp up the threat of disorder or violence, to change the factual context, and therefore effectively act as a veto."It added: "This is not balanced or fair to us; it is depriving us, potentially on a permanent basis, of what we have been lawfully granted for Sunday, with no guarantee this outcome will be replicated even if the Applicant's case is ultimately found to be without any merit whatsoever."The letter concluded: "We would ask the court not to take this unprecedented and extraordinary step, which we are advised is unheard of and has hitherto not ever occurred."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Parades Commission has determined that the parade can depart Drumcree Parish Church no later than 08:00 BST on SundayEarlier the judge highlighted that the information provided to the court from the PSNI has "promoted further enquiries" and "further time would be of benefit to the court.""In my view it would be contrary to justice and unwise to proceed to make a decision in the absence of information in relation to the issues I have identified."She said the important date for the Orange Order was July 5 and therefore there "is no prejudice in adjourning for a short period to allow this case to be prepared by all parties ."Rather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the Parades Commission had said the march could depart no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants , externalrather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. No bands or supporters are allowed.According to the Drumcree Catholic Church parish website, external, Mass takes place at 08:30 on Sundays in the church of St John the Baptist on the Garvaghy Road. When asked by BBC News NI if Mass time had been taken into consideration, the Parades Commission said commissioners "recognise that the timings set out in the determination" should allow the church service "to proceed as normal".Image source, Catholic Communications Office archiveImage caption, Archbishop Eamon Martin said his thoughts were with those affected by the situation 'March going to clash with Massgoers'In a statement on Saturday afternoon Archbishop Eamon Martin called for "prayers and support for a peaceful resolution to complex Garvaghy Road situation".The Catholic primate said he shared the "sense of shock and disappointment of so many people at recent developments"."I also appeal for support for the patient use of solely lawful and democratic processes to resolve this deeply complex and emotive situation."Fr Peter Clarke, from St John the Baptist in Portadown, said he was concerned the march would "clash" with parishioners coming and going from the church.He said he had emailed the commission to express his concerns and stated he "doesn't know how they came to" their conclusion.Parishioners at St Patrick's Church on William Street are also likely to be affected ahead of the 10:00 service, according to the priest.He added "tensions are high" in the community, and said he will be addressing the situation during Sunday's service.The decision to give the go-ahead for the parade came after the five-person Parades Commission, led by Prof Evelyn Collins, held face-to-face talks with the Orange Order earlier this week, and a separate meeting with the residents' coalition.Senior police officers were also consulted about the planned parade.Within the 31-paragraph determination by the Parades Commission, details were revealed of conversations held with the PSNI.The document stated: "The police made both written and oral submissions, indicating that they, at the time of making them, had no information indicating that the parade would result in disorder or violence."The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it had activated "mutual aid arrangements to support contingency planning for a policing operation" in Portadown on Sunday.It is understood about 200 officers are coming from Scotland.When did the Drumcree dispute begin?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, British soldiers erect a security fence at Drumcree Church in July 2002The Parades Commission has been in the political spotlight since its previous Drumcree determination was quashed in the High Court in August.A review of the commission has since been ordered by the Northern Ireland Office.The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time.Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders.When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order over the past three decades.

schema.headline: Orange Orderparade along Garvaghy Road halted after injuction granted

title: Manchester City charges: Khaldoon Al Mubarak confident club will prove innocence
description: Figure caption, Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man CityByPaul BattisonBBC Sport Journalist and Ffion WynneBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 7 hou
body: Figure caption, Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man CityByPaul BattisonBBC Sport Journalist and Ffion WynneBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 7 hours agoManchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak says he is still confident of proving the club's innocence after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.On Friday, it was announced City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them and Al Mubarak has responded with a letter to fans on the club's website. "Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said."Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. "But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine. Al Mubarak, who was appointed as City's chairman after their 2008 takeover, also said his club was being "undermined". "While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed," he added."There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."Meanwhile, Christian Purslow, a former Liverpool managing director and Aston Villa chief executive, who also held a senior role at Chelsea, said the City case could begin a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game".Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Purslow appeared alongside football law expert Paul Gilroy KC, who described the case as a "seismic moment for world football".Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss. Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3m."Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated. Let's say the team that finished 18th would've finished 17th if Manchester City weren't there. And they, of course, suffered huge loss."If you add all those claims up, over nine years, and that's just in the Premier League, you can see that the potential here for this to spiral out of control is huge."Gilroy added that, so far, four clubs have put in protective claims "reserving the right to claim compensation if City are found guilty".'Very unsettling for football fans'The news, broken by the Athletic,, external came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months after a hearing by an independent commission concluded.No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment.Manchester City declined to comment on whether they had been found guilty, instead providing a statement which read: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality."The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has urged the Premier League to come to a quick resolution.She told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think most football fans will be feeling that this is not a good moment for football as a whole and I think Manchester City fans will be feeling very, very anxious about what happens next."It's very unsettling for football fans and I hope that it can be resolved as swiftly as possible."I will obviously look very closely as what comes out of this but we can't apply those rules for the Premier League. They have got to do it themselves and are going to have to resolve this as swiftly as possible - not just for the sake of Manchester City but for the sake of football."Figure caption, What do Man City charges mean and what happens next?Former chairman Bernstein feels 'absolutely awful'City won eight trophies in the period covered by the case, including three Premier League titles, three EFL Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup.The charges cover the managerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club at the end of last season after 10 years in charge.David Bernstein, who was Manchester City chairman from 1998-2003, told Times Radio he felt "absolutely awful" on hearing the news of City being found guilty - but admitted any punishment would have to be "more drastic" than a fine. "To see all this tarnished in this way is very sad," he said."I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who've stayed with the club through thick and thin."This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because you've got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it's just not viable."The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster, not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial."He continued: "I can't give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty."All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that."Meanwhile, singer-songwriter Noel Gallagher says he is "shocked" at the news and it is "quite sad" for players and fans."A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges," the Oasis star and City fan said on the Let Me Talk podcast."So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we've been found guilty. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players."Follow Manchester City on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical City contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about City

title: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age
description: Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.
body: Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.According to the Booksellers Association, the number of independent book shops in the UK and Ireland is now at its highest level since 2012, with 1,086 stores in 2025 - up from a record low of 867 in 2016.But what is the reality of life as a small bookseller, competing with Amazon, finding new customers, and actually trying to make a profit?Sally Flint, 57, opened The Book Stop in Brigg, North Lincolnshire, just six weeks ago.So far, the "dream" move is living up to her expectations, but it has not been without its challenges. "It's brilliant. It's just like it's Christmas Day every day, because you're just with other people who love books and love reading," she says.However, to make her dream possible, Sally is working up to 14 hours a day.She describes her first foray into bookselling as a "steep learning curve", but says she is having "lots of fun along the way".

schema.headline: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age
